extracted.intended_audience: general readers, romance authors, and scholars interested in the romance novel genre
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and prescriptive overview of the romance novel as a literary genre: definitions, core requirements, common tropes and subgenres, format/length conventions, and publishing-line constraints. Useful for readers, writers, editors, and scholars seeking standards and expectations for romance fiction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main-plot core requirement (RWA)
rubrics_metrics.description: The main plot of a mass-market romance novel must revolve about the two people as they develop romantic love for each other and work to build a relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both the conflict and the climax of the novel should be directly related to that core theme of developing a romantic relationship, although the novel can also contain subplots that do not specifically relate to the main characters' romantic love.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotionally satisfying, optimistic ending (RWA)
rubrics_metrics.description: A romance novel must have an 'emotionally satisfying and optimistic ending.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formal requirement in many definitions of the genre (e.g., Romance Writers of America). While many books considered romance deviate from this rule, the conventional mass-market expectation is an optimistic resolution for the central relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship as the core of the book (publisher/editor definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance must make the 'romantic relationship between the hero and the heroine ... the core of the book.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The romantic relationship—not peripheral plotlines—should be the driving force shaping scenes, character decisions, and emotional stakes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict and climax tied to the romance
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the conflict and the climax should be directly related to the core theme of developing a romantic relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspense, obstacles, and climax are evaluated by how they affect the protagonists' relationship; events that are unrelated to that arc should remain as subplots or backstory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader expectation / foreknowledge (genre contract)
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers approach romance novels knowing the trajectory: protagonists meet and fall in love, are drawn apart by conflict, and are reunited by the end—often married or planning marriage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'contract' shapes pacing and plot placement (e.g., early meeting, mid-story separation, late reconciliation) and can influence expected page-by-page beats (Joan Schulhafer reference to being back together by page 192).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escapism as an audience expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Escapism is important to the genre; romances often present worlds where everyday interruptions and hardships are minimized to focus on the relationship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors and readers may expect a tone and setting that allow emotional immersion (quoted observation: 'The phone never rings, the baby never cries and the rent's never overdue in romances').

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral valence: rewarding protagonists who are 'good'
rubrics_metrics.description: In general, romance novels reward characters who are good people and penalize those who are evil; couples who fight for and believe in their relationship will likely be rewarded with unconditional love.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This moral framework affects character arcs and the types of redemption or punishment scenes authors include; consider how actions align with genre expectations of justice and reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Centrality of protagonists' relationship to all major decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The protagonists' developing relationship must impact each decision they make and increase tension in genres like romantic suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For romantic suspense specifically: the relationship should propel the suspense and be affected by the mystery/intrigue; events of suspense must directly affect the relationship and move the story forward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement (often assumed) that protagonists meet early
rubrics_metrics.description: Some authors/readers/publishers expect protagonists to meet early in the story so the romance can develop on-page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a contested expectation (some argue for it as a rule; others allow deviations), but it frequently appears in line-level guidelines and craft advice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Happy/optimistic ending debate and allowable deviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the stricter definition requires a happy/optimistic ending, many widely read books considered romance deviate from this rule; exceptions exist when the focus remains on the romantic relationship even if the ending is not conventionally happy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers, contests, and marketing channels may enforce the happy-ending rule more strictly than literary classification or academic discussion does.

rubrics_metrics.name: No intrinsic limits on setting, time period, or controversial topics
rubrics_metrics.description: A romance novel can be set in any time period and location; even controversial subjects (date rape, domestic violence, addiction, disability) may be addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subgenre labeling (historical, paranormal, sci-fi, contemporary, etc.) is typically used to signal the setting/subject choices to readers and retailers; inclusion of controversial subjects may affect line acceptance and reader expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category romance length and paring to essentials
rubrics_metrics.description: Category romances are short (usually no more than 200 pages, or about 55,000 words) and authors 'must pare the story down to its essentials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subplots and minor characters are eliminated or relegated to backstory; category lines expect concise plotting and tight focus on the central romance to fit line page/word limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category romance line identity and line-level guidelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Category romance lines each have a distinct identity (settings, time periods, levels of sensuality, types of conflict); publishers usually issue guidelines for each line specifying necessary elements to be included.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers targeting a particular line must follow its specific content and tone requirements (e.g., sensuality level, hero/heroine types, period detail). Lines publish a set number of titles monthly and may number books sequentially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Single-title romance length and format
rubrics_metrics.description: Single-title romances are longer (typically 350–400 pages, or 100,000–110,000 words) and are not part of a publisher's category line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Single-title novels allow more subplots and secondary characters, may be published less frequently per author, and remain on bookstore shelves at retailers' discretion; authors often write 1–1.5 books per year in this format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat/sensuality level varies by line/market
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance books vary across a spectrum—from chaste kisses to explicit erotic content—and many publishers maintain separate lines (or labels) that specify allowable levels of sexual content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting or writing for a line, observe its sensuality policy (e.g., Avon/Candlelight Ecstasy, Silhouette Desire, erotic vs. inspirational/Christian romance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Point-of-view and narrator expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Because women buy a large share of romance novels, most romances are told from a woman's viewpoint in either first or third person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: That viewpoint choice influences voice, internality, and focalization; authors should match POV to reader expectations for the subgenre/line.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tropes and stock devices as genre signals
rubrics_metrics.description: Romance frequently uses recognizable tropes (enemies to lovers, second chance, forced proximity, alpha male/helpless heroine archetypes, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tropes help signal a book's subgenre and meet reader expectations, but overuse creates redundancy; successful stories may subvert or freshen tropes to avoid feeling formulaic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical-subgenre fidelity (research/detail)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical romance often uses carefully researched historical detail as a major plot device to help readers understand the period (e.g., Regency settings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accuracy and period-specific detail are elements editors and readers expect in historical lines—failure to meet those expectations can reduce a book's credibility within that subgenre.

rubrics_metrics.name: Market/line editorial rules and decency codes (historical example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and reprint houses historically enforced 'decency codes' rejecting more explicit material; line editors set moral/content boundaries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should consult current publisher/line guidelines as these policies have shifted over time (e.g., some lines later waived requirements such as heroine virginity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of plot vs. character in subgenres (romantic suspense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some subgenres (romantic suspense) tend to be more plot-driven (mystery/intrigue) rather than character-driven, while still keeping the romance central.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the genre demands: ensure the mystery propels the relationship and vice versa; language may be 'cleaner' than in other romance subgenres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Line production/scheduling expectations
rubrics_metrics.description: Category romance lines publish a fixed number of books each month; books may be numbered sequentially and remain on shelves only until the next titles arrive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Writers for category publishers must meet tight schedules and adhere to line identity to be accepted and retained; distribution and page-count constraints are part of the acceptance criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diversity and representation growth (21st century expectation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the 21st century, romance has increasingly diversified main characters and plots to include identities previously underrepresented (disabled characters, autistic characters, LGBTQ protagonists).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While inclusion is growing, representation norms and sensitivity considerations may affect editorial decisions and reception; authentic, respectful portrayal is increasingly expected by readers and critics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding redundancy and originality expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Market saturation with similar plots led readers to complain of redundancy; editors/readers reward novelty and broadened characterization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To succeed, authors should refresh familiar tropes, expand hero/heroine types, and avoid formulaic repetition that reduces reader engagement and return rates.
